lessons.title: Building a Queen Excluder Frame
lessons.body: A queen excluder keeps the queen out of the honey supers so she doesn't lay eggs there. You can buy one, but making your own saves money and lets you fit it to your hive. You need a wooden frame that fits between the brood box and the super. Use 2 cm thick timber, about 10 cm wide. Cut four pieces: two long sides equal to the hive's length (usually 48 cm) and two short sides equal to the width (usually 40 cm). Nail or screw them into a rectangle. The critical part is the mesh: use galvanized wire mesh with holes exactly 4.2 mm (or 4.1â4.5 mm). If holes are too big, the queen passes; too small, workers can't pass. You can find this mesh at agricultural supply shops or order it online. Cut the mesh 2 cm larger than the frame opening on all sides. Staple it to the frame using a staple gun or hammer and fencing staples, pulling it tight so it doesn't sag. Fold the edges over and staple again. For an African context, if you can't find 4.2 mm mesh, you can use a piece of plastic queen excluder cut to size, but ensure it's secured flat. Test the excluder by placing it on a hive and watching: workers should move through freely, but the queen (larger thorax) cannot. Check for gaps at corners; bees will glue them with propolis, but large gaps let the queen through. Paint the wooden frame with linseed oil or leave untreated; avoid toxic paints. In hot climates, metal mesh can get hot, so consider a wooden rim to shade it. This component costs little and lasts years if kept dry. Always remove the excluder during winter or when not using supers, as bees may cluster and starve if they can't reach honey.

lessons.title: Constructing a Feeder: Boardman and Division Board
lessons.body: Feeders are essential for feeding sugar syrup during dearth periods or to stimulate brood. Two common types are the Boardman feeder and the division board feeder. The Boardman feeder is an entrance feeder: a inverted jar screwed onto a wooden base that sits at the hive entrance. To build one, you need a glass jar (1 litre) with a metal lid. Punch 6â8 small holes (1 mm) in the lid. Make a wooden base from 2 cm thick timber, about 15 cm x 10 cm, with a raised rim to hold the jar upside down. The base has a slot that fits the hive entrance. When inverted, syrup drips slowly, and bees feed from the base. This feeder is cheap and easy, but in hot African climates, syrup can ferment or attract ants. The division board feeder replaces a frame inside the hive. Build a box that fits the brood chamber dimensions (e.g., 48 cm long, 5 cm wide, 25 cm deep). Use plywood or timber. Make a float from thin wood or styrofoam to prevent bees from drowning. Fill with syrup and place it in the hive where a frame would go. Bees access it from the top. This feeder is safer from robbers and ants. For both, use 1:1 sugar syrup (1 kg sugar to 1 litre water) for stimulation, or 2:1 for winter stores. In Africa, where cane sugar is available, this is practical. Clean feeders regularly to prevent mold. Build the division board from untreated pine; avoid treated wood. Seal joints with beeswax or food-grade silicone. A well-made feeder costs less than buying and can be repaired. Always provide a landing area for bees. In dry areas, also provide water nearby.

lessons.title: Building a Pollen Trap
lessons.body: A pollen trap collects pollen from foragers' legs as they enter the hive. This is valuable for selling or feeding. The simplest is a bottom-mounted trap that fits under the brood box. You need a wooden frame that matches the hive base, about 5 cm high. The key component is a screen with 5 mm holes (hardware cloth) that bees must squeeze through, knocking off pollen pellets. Below the screen, a drawer with a fine mesh (1 mm) collects the pollen. Build the frame from 2 cm timber. Cut a piece of 5 mm mesh to fit the hive entrance area. The bees enter through a 2 cm gap, then must pass through the mesh to reach the brood chamber. Pollen falls through the mesh into a tray. Make the tray from plywood with a fine screen bottom for ventilation. It should slide in and out for easy collection. In Africa, use locally available materials: mosquito netting for the fine mesh, and metal gauze for the 5 mm. Ensure the trap doesn't block the entrance completely; leave a side escape for drones and workers to bypass if needed. Collect pollen every 2â3 days to prevent mold. Dry pollen in shade before storing. A good trap can collect 50â100 g per day in strong season. But don't leave it on all year; pollen is essential for brood. Use it for 1â2 weeks, then remove. Build two traps so you can alternate. This component requires precision: holes too large let pollen pass, too small trap bees. Test with a few bees. In hot climates, place the trap in shade to avoid overheating. Clean regularly to prevent pests.

lessons.title: Constructing a Swarm Trap or Bait Hive
lessons.body: A swarm trap is a lightweight box used to attract and capture wild swarms. In Africa, where swarms are abundant, this is a cheap way to get bees. Use a box made from plywood or thin timber, about 40 cm x 30 cm x 25 cm. It should have a volume of about 30â40 litres, similar to a small hive. Cut a 3 cm entrance hole near the top. Inside, place 3â4 frames with foundation or just top bars. The trap should be watertight but ventilated. Use a lid that overlaps. To attract bees, bait the trap with lemongrass oil or old comb. Rub the inside with beeswax. Place the trap in a shady tree, 3â5 metres high, facing east to catch morning sun. In African savanna, hang traps near water and flowering trees. Check traps weekly during swarming season (often after rains). When bees move in, they will start building comb. Once established, close the entrance at night and move the trap to your apiary. Then transfer the frames to a permanent hive. Build the trap from untreated wood; avoid plywood with toxic glues. Use nails and exterior wood glue. Add a small landing board. For durability, paint the outside with light-coloured paint. A good swarm trap can be made from a discarded wooden crate. Ensure it's secure against monkeys and honey badgers. In some regions, use a traditional log hive as a trap. Always get permission if hanging on someone's land. This component costs almost nothing and can build your apiary quickly.

lessons.title: Building a Nuc Box for Splits
lessons.body: A nucleus (nuc) box is a small hive used to start new colonies from splits or to rear queens. It typically holds 4â5 frames. Build it from 2 cm thick timber, with dimensions to fit standard frames. For a 5-frame nuc, internal dimensions: 48 cm long, 20 cm wide, 25 cm deep. Cut two long sides (48 cm), two short sides (20 cm), a bottom (48x20 cm), and a lid. Assemble with nails and glue. The entrance should be 2 cm high and 5 cm wide, with a reducer to control traffic. Add a screened ventilation hole (5 cm diameter) on the side, covered with mesh. Inside, use frames with foundation or starter strips. Nuc boxes are essential for making splits: you take 2â3 frames of brood, 1 frame of honey, and 1 frame of bees from a strong hive, place them in the nuc, and add a new queen or let them raise one. In Africa, nuc boxes can be made from cheap plywood or even cardboard for temporary use, but wood lasts longer. Paint the outside with light colour. Place the nuc in a shady spot. Feed with sugar syrup until established. A nuc box allows you to increase your apiary without buying full hives. Build several so you can manage multiple splits. Ensure frames fit snugly to prevent burr comb. Use a follower board to adjust space. Check for pests like ants; place legs in oil cans. This component is simple and can be built in an hour.

lessons.title: Constructing a Winterization Wrap or Cozy
lessons.body: In many African regions, winters are mild, but in highlands or deserts, nights can be cold. A winterization wrap or cozy helps bees maintain brood temperature and reduces stress. Use breathable materials like burlap, hessian, or old blankets. Do not use plastic, which traps moisture. Cut a piece of burlap to wrap around the hive, leaving the entrance open. Secure with rope or tape. For extra insulation, add a layer of dry grass or straw between the wrap and the hive. In cold areas, you can build a wooden outer shell with insulation. Use 2 cm timber to make a box that fits over the hive with 5 cm gap, fill the gap with sawdust or vermiculite. The top can have a cushion of dry leaves. Ensure ventilation: drill 2 cm holes near the top to let moisture escape. In Africa, many beekeepers use a simple quilt box: a shallow box filled with wood shavings or dry grass, placed on top of the hive under the lid. This absorbs moisture and insulates. Build it from plywood, 10 cm deep, with a mesh bottom. The bees propolize it, but it's effective. Winterization is not needed in tropical lowlands, but in areas with frost, it can save colonies. Also reduce the entrance to 1 cm to keep out cold and robbers. Provide extra honey stores (2â3 frames) before winter. The wrap should be removed in spring. In hot climates, a reflective cover can reduce heat. Always allow ventilation; condensation kills bees. This component is cheap and can be made from recycled materials. Test the temperature inside: if it's too hot, remove insulation.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a queen excluder?
options: A) To keep the queen from laying eggs in honey supers
B) To prevent drones from entering the hive
C) To keep worker bees inside
quiz.explanation: The queen excluder allows workers through but blocks the larger queen, so she cannot lay eggs in the honey supers.

quiz.q: What is the correct mesh size for a queen excluder?
quiz.explanation: 4.2 mm holes allow worker bees to pass but are too small for the queen's thorax.

quiz.q: Which material is best for the mesh of a queen excluder?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized wire mesh is durable and holds the precise 4.2 mm holes needed.

quiz.q: What is a common problem if the queen excluder has gaps at the corners?
options: B) The queen can pass through
quiz.explanation: Gaps larger than 4.2 mm allow the queen to squeeze through, defeating the purpose.

quiz.q: Why should you remove the queen excluder during winter?
options: B) To allow the queen to move with the cluster
quiz.explanation: In winter, the cluster moves to honey stores; if the queen is trapped below, she may freeze or starve.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a Boardman feeder?
options: A) It fits inside the hive
B) It is cheap and easy to build
quiz.explanation: The Boardman feeder uses a jar and a simple wooden base, making it inexpensive and simple.

quiz.q: What size holes should be punched in the lid of a Boardman feeder jar?
quiz.explanation: 1 mm holes allow syrup to drip slowly without flooding.

quiz.q: What is a division board feeder?
options: A) A feeder that hangs outside the entrance
B) A feeder that replaces a frame inside the hive
C) A feeder made from a plastic bottle
D) A feeder placed on top of the hive
quiz.explanation: It is a box that fits in the brood chamber like a frame, providing syrup inside the hive.

quiz.q: Why is a float used in a division board feeder?
options: A) To keep the syrup cool
B) To prevent bees from drowning
C) To measure the syrup level
quiz.explanation: A float gives bees a landing surface so they don't fall into the syrup and drown.

quiz.q: What sugar-to-water ratio is used for stimulating brood in a feeder?
quiz.explanation: 1:1 syrup mimics nectar flow and stimulates the queen to lay eggs.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a pollen trap?
options: A) To collect pollen from foragers
B) To keep pollen out of the hive
C) To feed pollen to bees
quiz.explanation: A pollen trap strips pollen pellets from bees' legs as they enter the hive.

quiz.q: What size holes are used in the screen of a pollen trap?
quiz.explanation: 5 mm holes force bees to squeeze through, knocking off pollen pellets.

quiz.q: How often should you collect pollen from a trap?
quiz.explanation: Collecting every 2â3 days prevents mold and keeps pollen fresh.

quiz.q: Why should a pollen trap not be left on all year?
options: B) Bees need pollen for brood rearing
quiz.explanation: Pollen is essential for brood; continuous trapping can weaken the colony.

quiz.q: What material can be used for the fine mesh in a pollen trap tray?
quiz.explanation: Mosquito netting is fine enough to hold pollen while allowing ventilation.

quiz.q: What is a swarm trap used for?
options: A) To catch and relocate wild swarms
quiz.explanation: A swarm trap is a box designed to attract and capture wild bee swarms.

quiz.q: What is a good bait for a swarm trap?
quiz.explanation: Lemongrass oil mimics the pheromone that attracts scout bees.

quiz.q: Where should a swarm trap be placed?
options: B) In a shady tree 3â5 m high
quiz.explanation: Shade and height protect the trap and make it more attractive to swarms.

quiz.q: What is the ideal volume for a swarm trap?
quiz.explanation: 30â40 litres is similar to a natural cavity and attractive to swarms.

quiz.q: When should you check swarm traps?
quiz.explanation: Weekly checks during swarming season allow you to catch swarms before they abscond.

quiz.q: What is a nuc box used for?
options: B) To start new colonies from splits
quiz.explanation: A nuc box is a small hive used to house a split or a new queen colony.

quiz.q: How many frames does a typical nuc box hold?
quiz.explanation: A standard nuc box holds 4â5 frames, enough for a small colony.

quiz.q: What is the internal length of a 5-frame nuc box?
quiz.explanation: 48 cm matches the length of standard frames, allowing them to fit.

quiz.q: Why should a nuc box have a ventilation hole?
options: B) To prevent overheating and moisture buildup
quiz.explanation: Ventilation prevents condensation and overheating, especially in hot climates.

quiz.q: What should you feed a new colony in a nuc box?
quiz.explanation: Sugar syrup provides energy until the colony has enough foragers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a winterization wrap?
options: A) To insulate the hive and reduce cold stress
quiz.explanation: A wrap helps bees maintain brood temperature and reduces stress in cold weather.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a winterization wrap?
quiz.explanation: Burlap is breathable and insulates without trapping moisture.

quiz.q: What is a quilt box used for in winter?
options: B) To absorb moisture and insulate
quiz.explanation: A quilt box filled with wood shavings absorbs moisture and adds insulation.

quiz.q: Why should you reduce the entrance in winter?
options: A) To keep out cold and robbers
B) To let more bees in
quiz.explanation: A smaller entrance helps the colony defend against robbers and reduces heat loss.

quiz.q: What is a sign that winterization is too hot for the bees?
quiz.explanation: Bearding outside indicates overheating; remove insulation or increase ventilation.
